newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia says needs two new refineries by 2000.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia says needs two new refineries by 2000.

text.p: Indonesia needs two more oil refineries by 2000 to meet burgeoning domestic demand for fuel products, the president-director of national oil company Pertamina said on Thursday.

Faisal Abda'oe told Reuters in an interview the new refineries should each have a capacity of 125,000 barrels per day (bpd) to help meet demand in Indonesia, Asia's sole member of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC).
"We are in a very risky situation when we compare the increase in domestic fuel products demand with our current refining capacity," Abda'oe said.

"We have told the government that by 2000 we should have in operation two new refineries with a capacity of 125,000 bpd each. If not, we are going to see very high imports of fuel products, especially diesel oil and kerosene," he said.
"Pertamina is ready to build new refineries if the government gives us the green light."
Pertamina now has eight refineries with a combined capacity of 989,500 bpd. There are no private refineries.
Pertamina said on Monday it would import about 10 million kilolitres of fuel products in fiscal 1997/98 (April-March), up from an estimated seven million kilolitres in 1996/97.

"In 1997/98 domestic fuel products production is expected to be around 40.9 million kilolitres, while consumption will be 50.9 million kilolitres. So, in 1997/98 there is a need to import around 10 million kilolitres," Pertamina director of supply Judosumardjo said on Monday.
Another Pertamina official said domestic fuel product consumption was estimated at 47.6 million kilolitres in 1996/97.

He said diesel oil consumption was expected to rise to 20.8 million kilolitres in fiscal 1997/98 from an estimated 19.2 million in 1996/97. Kerosene consumption was expected to rise to 9.9 million kilolitres in 1997/98 from 9.3 million, he said.
Abda'oe said Pertamina had urged private firms to build refineries two years ago, but none had been constructed.
Industry sources said private firms were not keen on setting up refineries because processing margins were thin and they had to sell fuel products at prices determined by the government.
Abda'oe said Pertamina would raise the capacity of its refineries through upgrading and removing bottlenecks in projects.
Pertamina is constructing a 65,000-bpd capacity crude oil distillation unit at the Balikpapan I refinery in Kalimantan through an upgradation project costing some $400 million.

"This project is aimed at increasing the capacity of the Balikpapan I refinery to 65,000 bpd from around 45,000 bpd at the moment," Pertamina's junior processing director Samto Utomo told Reuters. "This project is expected to be completed in May or June this year."
He said a project to remove bottlenecks was underway at the Cilacap refinery in Central Java to increase its capacity to 348,000 bpd from 300,000 bpd.
"The Cilacap debottlenecking project is expected to be completed by the end of 1998 or in early 1999," Utomo said.
He said, however, the increase in the consumption of fuel products would continue to outstrip supply despite the projects.
